A multi-country Bayesian macro model

Structure, results and forecasts across eight estimated systems

What this is

This is the handout form of overview_presentation.qmd. The same source also renders as a slide deck (overview_presentation.html); this version is meant to be read end to end rather than presented. Every figure is derived from the cached fits — see the Reference section for which report argues each point in full.

A multi-country Bayesian simultaneous-equations macro model, built on the koma package.

  • 11 euro-area economies + the US, quarterly, 2000–2024
  • Every country’s behavioural equations and accounting identities estimated in one system, so cross-country effects are jointly identified rather than bolted on afterwards
  • Five estimated systems, each a deliberate step: 1 → 2a → 2b → 2c → 2d, plus two extension blocks (3a, 3b)
  • Everything below comes from cached fits and is reproducible from the repo

The one thing that governs all of it: every system spends observations on parameters. df = T − k. Nearly every result in this deck is downstream of that number.

The equation template, stage by stage

Every stage is written once for a generic country cc and applied to each economy, so a system with 68 stochastic equations still has only a handful of distinct forms. That is what makes the stages comparable at all, and it is why this section is the right place to start: read the eight blocks below and you have read the whole model.

The equations are extracted from the fitted systems, not transcribed – scratch/overview_build.R takes one representative entity’s equations off each sys_eq and replaces its own prefix with cc. A block below therefore cannot describe a specification that was not estimated. The intercept and the four COVID impulse dummies are suppressed throughout for readability; .L(1) is a one-quarter lag; == marks an identity, imposed during estimation rather than fitted.

Each block ends with what changed relative to the stage it descends from, which is not always the previous row: stage 3a extends stage 2b, and stage 3d puts stage 3a’s block on stage 2d’s partition. The diffs are computed from the two templates rather than written by hand. They compare regressor names, so a change of identity weight alone – an expenditure share re-derived on a different sample, say – does not appear as a change; the weights are printed in full above each diff for exactly that reason.

On the identity weights. Every one of them is computed from the data, and none is estimated — an identity fixes entries of koma’s Gamma matrix rather than being fitted, so its weights are a specification choice. Each block below says which rule set its own. Two properties are shared across all of them. First, weights are rounded to three decimals so the equation strings stay readable; that is safe precisely because they are a choice rather than a constraint the data has to satisfy. Second, and for the same reason, koma performs no identity-consistency check at all — a wrong weight is silent, not an error — so stage2_preflight()’s identity_consistency() does the arithmetic koma does not, recomputing every identity from the panel and reporting its worst error (on the stage-2c panel: 23 exact identities, worst 1.05e-13).

Stage 1 — 11 countries, estimated separately (k, T, df are per country)

k = 12, T = 78, df = 66 · 2000Q1–2019Q4 · 6 stochastic + 2 identities

cc_consumption ~ cc_gdp + cc_consumption.L(1)
cc_investment ~ cc_gdp + cc_investment.L(1)
cc_exports ~ row_gdp + cc_exports.L(1)
cc_imports ~ cc_domestic_demand + cc_imports.L(1)
cc_prices ~ eur_usd + oil_price + cc_prices.L(1)
cc_long_rate ~ cc_prices + ea_policy_rate + cc_long_rate.L(1)

Identities:

cc_gdp == 0.937*cc_domestic_demand + 0.369*cc_exports - 0.314*cc_imports
cc_domestic_demand == 0.585*cc_consumption + 0.211*cc_investment + 0.204*cc_government

Where the weights come from:

  • cc_gdp and cc_domestic_demand — average expenditure shares, each one the mean of the period-by-period level ratio (mean(cc_exports / cc_gdp), not the ratio of the means) over this stage’s own estimation window, rounded to 3dp. Computed on levels and used in growth space deliberately: log-linearising an accounting identity turns it into a share-weighted sum of the components’ growth rates, so the level shares are the growth-rate coefficients. The GDP identity holds only up to the national-accounts statistical discrepancy (2–6%, wider for Ireland), and is reported but never flagged for that reason; the consumption/investment/government split sums to exactly 1, because domestic demand is their sum. expenditure_shares().

Stage 2a — DE + FR, one joint system

k = 19, T = 78, df = 59 · 2000Q1–2019Q4 · 13 stochastic + 8 identities

cc_consumption ~ cc_gdp + cc_consumption.L(1)
cc_investment ~ cc_gdp + cc_long_rate + cc_investment.L(1)
cc_exports ~ cc_foreign_demand + cc_exports.L(1)
cc_imports ~ cc_domestic_demand + cc_imports.L(1)
cc_prices ~ eur_usd + oil_price + cc_prices.L(1)
cc_long_rate ~ cc_prices + ea_policy_rate + cc_gdp + cc_long_rate.L(1)

Identities:

cc_gdp == 0.937*cc_domestic_demand + 0.369*cc_exports - 0.314*cc_imports
cc_domestic_demand == 0.585*cc_consumption + 0.211*cc_investment + 0.204*cc_government
cc_foreign_demand == 0.065*fr_gdp + 0.935*row_gdp

Where the weights come from:

  • cc_gdp and cc_domestic_demand — average expenditure shares, each one the mean of the period-by-period level ratio (mean(cc_exports / cc_gdp), not the ratio of the means) over this stage’s own estimation window, rounded to 3dp. Computed on levels and used in growth space deliberately: log-linearising an accounting identity turns it into a share-weighted sum of the components’ growth rates, so the level shares are the growth-rate coefficients. The GDP identity holds only up to the national-accounts statistical discrepancy (2–6%, wider for Ireland), and is reported but never flagged for that reason; the consumption/investment/government split sums to exactly 1, because domestic demand is their sum. expenditure_shares().
  • cc_foreign_demand — bilateral trade weights from the ECB WTS matrix, restricted to the modelled partners and loaded on partner GDP. Whatever share of trade the partition does not model is folded onto the exogenous row_gdp residual rather than dropped, so the weights still sum to 1 and the index stays a proper weighted average of growth rates — here 0.935, so over half the index is an assumption that the unmodelled world grows like world GDP. stage2_linkage_weights().

Changed from Stage 1:

  • new: cc_foreign_demand
  • cc_investment: +cc_long_rate
  • cc_exports: +cc_foreign_demand, −row_gdp
  • cc_long_rate: +cc_gdp

Stage 2b — 11 countries, one joint system

k = 76, T = 98, df = 22 · 2000Q1–2024Q4 · 68 stochastic + 35 identities

cc_consumption ~ cc_gdp + cc_consumption.L(1)
cc_investment ~ cc_gdp + cc_long_rate + cc_investment.L(1)
cc_exports ~ cc_foreign_demand + cc_exports.L(1)
cc_imports ~ cc_domestic_demand + cc_imports.L(1)
cc_prices ~ eur_usd + oil_price + cc_prices.L(1)
cc_long_rate ~ cc_prices + ea_policy_rate + cc_gdp + cc_long_rate.L(1)

Identities:

cc_gdp == 0.937*cc_domestic_demand + 0.382*cc_exports - 0.33*cc_imports
cc_domestic_demand == 0.733*cc_consumption + 0.267*cc_investment
cc_foreign_demand == 0.041*at_gdp + 0.04*be_gdp + 0.033*es_gdp + 0.065*fr_gdp + 0.025*ie_gdp + 0.052*it_gdp + 0.074*nl_gdp + 0.098*us_gdp + 0.572*row_gdp

Where the weights come from:

  • cc_gdp and cc_domestic_demand — average expenditure shares, each one the mean of the period-by-period level ratio (mean(cc_exports / cc_gdp), not the ratio of the means) over this stage’s own estimation window, rounded to 3dp. Computed on levels and used in growth space deliberately: log-linearising an accounting identity turns it into a share-weighted sum of the components’ growth rates, so the level shares are the growth-rate coefficients. The GDP identity holds only up to the national-accounts statistical discrepancy (2–6%, wider for Ireland), and is reported but never flagged for that reason; without government the domestic-demand split is deliberately inexact — the two shares are renormalised over what is left. expenditure_shares().
  • cc_foreign_demand — bilateral trade weights from the ECB WTS matrix, restricted to the modelled partners and loaded on partner GDP. Whatever share of trade the partition does not model is folded onto the exogenous row_gdp residual rather than dropped, so the weights still sum to 1 and the index stays a proper weighted average of growth rates — here 0.572, so over half the index is an assumption that the unmodelled world grows like world GDP. stage2_linkage_weights().

  • cc_domestic_demand: −cc_government
  • cc_foreign_demand — partner set follows the partition

Stage 2c — 11 countries, four refinements

k = 76, T = 98, df = 22 · 2000Q1–2024Q4 · 68 stochastic + 46 identities

cc_consumption ~ cc_gdp + cc_long_rate + cc_consumption.L(1)
cc_investment ~ cc_gdp + cc_long_rate + cc_investment.L(1)
cc_exports ~ cc_foreign_demand + cc_exports.L(1)
cc_imports ~ cc_domestic_demand + cc_imports.L(1)
cc_prices ~ eur_usd + oil_price + cc_gdp + cc_prices.L(1)
cc_spread ~ cc_prices + cc_gdp + cc_spread.L(1)

Identities:

cc_gdp == 0.937*cc_domestic_demand + 0.382*cc_exports - 0.33*cc_imports
cc_domestic_demand == 0.733*cc_consumption + 0.267*cc_investment
cc_foreign_demand == 0.041*at_imports + 0.04*be_imports + 0.033*es_imports + 0.065*fr_imports + 0.025*ie_imports + 0.052*it_imports + 0.074*nl_imports + 0.098*us_imports + 0.572*row_gdp
cc_long_rate == 1*cc_spread + 1*ea_policy_rate

Where the weights come from:

  • cc_gdp and cc_domestic_demand — average expenditure shares, each one the mean of the period-by-period level ratio (mean(cc_exports / cc_gdp), not the ratio of the means) over this stage’s own estimation window, rounded to 3dp. Computed on levels and used in growth space deliberately: log-linearising an accounting identity turns it into a share-weighted sum of the components’ growth rates, so the level shares are the growth-rate coefficients. The GDP identity holds only up to the national-accounts statistical discrepancy (2–6%, wider for Ireland), and is reported but never flagged for that reason; without government the domestic-demand split is deliberately inexact — the two shares are renormalised over what is left. expenditure_shares().
  • cc_foreign_demand — bilateral trade weights from the ECB WTS matrix, restricted to the modelled partners and loaded on partner imports. Whatever share of trade the partition does not model is folded onto the exogenous row_gdp residual rather than dropped, so the weights still sum to 1 and the index stays a proper weighted average of growth rates — here 0.572, so over half the index is an assumption that the unmodelled world grows like world GDP. stage2_linkage_weights().
  • cc_long_rate — both weights imposed at exactly 1: a sovereign yield is the policy path plus a term premium, so there is nothing to estimate. This is a rate/none identity, a literal linear combination of levels rather than of growth rates, and identity_consistency() checks it in that space. Note it has two sides — the identity string and the cc_spread series the panel builder constructs — and both derive the policy rate from policy_rate_map(), because when they disagreed the US identity was silently violated by the whole EA–US policy-rate gap (up to 3.25pp).

Changed from Stage 2b:

  • new: cc_spread
  • cc_consumption: +cc_long_rate
  • cc_prices: +cc_gdp
  • cc_long_rate — now an identity: +cc_spread, −cc_prices, −cc_gdp, −cc_long_rate.L(1)
  • cc_foreign_demand — partner set follows the partition

Stage 2d — 6 entities: DE FR IT US CN + REU bloc

k = 46, T = 78, df = 32 · 2005Q1–2024Q4 · 38 stochastic + 25 identities

cc_consumption ~ cc_gdp + cc_long_rate + cc_consumption.L(1)
cc_investment ~ cc_gdp + cc_long_rate + cc_investment.L(1)
cc_exports ~ cc_foreign_demand + cc_exports.L(1)
cc_imports ~ cc_domestic_demand + cc_imports.L(1)
cc_prices ~ eur_usd + oil_price + cc_gdp + cc_prices.L(1)
cc_spread ~ cc_prices + cc_gdp + cc_spread.L(1)

Identities:

cc_gdp == 0.932*cc_domestic_demand + 0.406*cc_exports - 0.348*cc_imports
cc_domestic_demand == 0.731*cc_consumption + 0.269*cc_investment
cc_foreign_demand == 0.065*fr_imports + 0.052*it_imports + 0.098*us_imports + 0.104*cn_imports + 0.225*reu_imports + 0.456*row_gdp
cc_long_rate == 1*cc_spread + 1*ea_policy_rate

Where the weights come from:

  • cc_gdp and cc_domestic_demand — average expenditure shares, each one the mean of the period-by-period level ratio (mean(cc_exports / cc_gdp), not the ratio of the means) over this stage’s own estimation window, rounded to 3dp. Computed on levels and used in growth space deliberately: log-linearising an accounting identity turns it into a share-weighted sum of the components’ growth rates, so the level shares are the growth-rate coefficients. The GDP identity holds only up to the national-accounts statistical discrepancy (2–6%, wider for Ireland), and is reported but never flagged for that reason; without government the domestic-demand split is deliberately inexact — the two shares are renormalised over what is left. expenditure_shares().
  • cc_foreign_demand — bilateral trade weights from the ECB WTS matrix, restricted to the modelled partners and loaded on partner imports. Whatever share of trade the partition does not model is folded onto the exogenous row_gdp residual rather than dropped, so the weights still sum to 1 and the index stays a proper weighted average of growth rates — here 0.456, the smallest residual of any stage, because the US and China are modelled partners here. The reu row is the bloc’s own trade weight, aggregated from its members. stage2_linkage_weights().
  • cc_long_rate — both weights imposed at exactly 1: a sovereign yield is the policy path plus a term premium, so there is nothing to estimate. This is a rate/none identity, a literal linear combination of levels rather than of growth rates, and identity_consistency() checks it in that space. Note it has two sides — the identity string and the cc_spread series the panel builder constructs — and both derive the policy rate from policy_rate_map(), because when they disagreed the US identity was silently violated by the whole EA–US policy-rate gap (up to 3.25pp).
  • The reu bloc’s own weights are member-weighted averages, not the bloc series’ own ratios. bloc_expenditure_shares() averages the seven members’ shares; taking mean(reu_exports / reu_gdp) directly would give 1.337 against a true 0.598, because every bloc series is a base-100 chain index and that ratio is just their relative growth since the base period. stage2_shares() aborts rather than falling back, so a bloc without bloc_weights fails loudly. Same rule for its HICP split — bloc_hicp_weights(), since there is no published reu basket to fetch.

Changed from Stage 2c:

  • cc_foreign_demand — partner set follows the partition

Stage 3a — Stage 2b + German labour/price block

k = 83, T = 98, df = 15 · 2000Q1–2024Q4 · 74 stochastic + 39 identities

cc_consumption ~ cc_gdp + cc_real_income + cc_consumption.L(1)
cc_investment ~ cc_gdp + cc_long_rate + cc_investment.L(1)
cc_exports ~ cc_foreign_demand + cc_export_prices + cc_foreign_prices + cc_exports.L(1)
cc_imports ~ cc_domestic_demand + cc_imports.L(1)
cc_long_rate ~ cc_prices + ea_policy_rate + cc_gdp + cc_long_rate.L(1)
cc_employment ~ cc_gdp + cc_employment.L(1)
cc_unemployment ~ cc_gdp + cc_unemployment.L(1)
cc_wages ~ cc_unemployment + cc_prices + cc_wages.L(1)
cc_nonenergy_prices ~ cc_ulc + cc_import_prices + cc_unemployment + cc_nonenergy_prices.L(1)
cc_energy_prices ~ oil_price + eur_usd + cc_energy_prices.L(1)
cc_import_prices ~ eur_usd + oil_price + cc_foreign_prices + cc_import_prices.L(1)
cc_export_prices ~ cc_ulc + cc_foreign_prices + cc_export_prices.L(1)

Identities:

cc_gdp == 0.937*cc_domestic_demand + 0.382*cc_exports - 0.33*cc_imports
cc_domestic_demand == 0.733*cc_consumption + 0.267*cc_investment
cc_foreign_demand == 0.041*at_gdp + 0.04*be_gdp + 0.033*es_gdp + 0.065*fr_gdp + 0.025*ie_gdp + 0.052*it_gdp + 0.074*nl_gdp + 0.098*us_gdp + 0.572*row_gdp
cc_productivity == 1*cc_gdp - 1*cc_employment
cc_ulc == 1*cc_wages - 1*cc_productivity
cc_prices == 0.891298*cc_nonenergy_prices + 0.108702*cc_energy_prices
cc_real_income == 1*cc_wages + 1*cc_employment - 1*cc_prices

Where the weights come from:

  • cc_gdp and cc_domestic_demand — average expenditure shares, each one the mean of the period-by-period level ratio (mean(cc_exports / cc_gdp), not the ratio of the means) over this stage’s own estimation window, rounded to 3dp. Computed on levels and used in growth space deliberately: log-linearising an accounting identity turns it into a share-weighted sum of the components’ growth rates, so the level shares are the growth-rate coefficients. The GDP identity holds only up to the national-accounts statistical discrepancy (2–6%, wider for Ireland), and is reported but never flagged for that reason; without government the domestic-demand split is deliberately inexact — the two shares are renormalised over what is left. expenditure_shares().
  • cc_foreign_demand — bilateral trade weights from the ECB WTS matrix, restricted to the modelled partners and loaded on partner GDP. Whatever share of trade the partition does not model is folded onto the exogenous row_gdp residual rather than dropped, so the weights still sum to 1 and the index stays a proper weighted average of growth rates — here 0.572, so over half the index is an assumption that the unmodelled world grows like world GDP. stage2_linkage_weights().
  • cc_prices — HICP basket shares fetched from Eurostat prc_hicp_inw and averaged over the estimation years (0.891 non-energy / 0.109 energy for Germany, not the 0.85/0.15 one would guess). Non-energy plus energy partitions the basket exactly — verified to sum to CP00 in every year 1996–2025 — whereas core plus energy leaves ~19% of the basket unaccounted for. This is the one weight that is genuinely an approximation: HICP weights are re-based annually (the German energy weight ranges 8.8–12.6% over the sample) while a koma identity weight is a constant, so hicp_weights() returns max_deviation to make the size of that approximation visible.
  • cc_productivity, cc_ulc, cc_real_income — imposed at exactly ±1, because these are definitions rather than estimates: unit labour cost is wages minus productivity, which telescopes through productivity == gdp − employment to nominal wage bill over real output. chain_weighted_index() sums diff(log(x)) * w without renormalising, which is what makes ±1 give exact differences — these reproduce to ~1e-13.

Changed from Stage 2b:

  • new: cc_employment, cc_unemployment, cc_wages, cc_nonenergy_prices, cc_energy_prices, cc_import_prices, cc_export_prices, cc_productivity, cc_ulc, cc_real_income
  • cc_consumption: +cc_real_income
  • cc_exports: +cc_export_prices, +cc_foreign_prices
  • cc_prices — now an identity: +cc_nonenergy_prices, +cc_energy_prices, −eur_usd, −oil_price, −cc_prices.L(1)

Stage 3b — Stage 3a + external/fiscal/financial

k = 90, T = 98, df = 8 · 2000Q1–2024Q4 · 79 stochastic + 43 identities

cc_consumption ~ cc_gdp + cc_real_income + cc_consumption.L(1)
cc_investment ~ cc_gdp + cc_long_rate + cc_credit + cc_investment.L(1)
cc_exports ~ cc_foreign_demand + cc_competitiveness + cc_exports.L(1)
cc_imports ~ cc_domestic_demand + cc_imports.L(1)
cc_employment ~ cc_gdp + cc_employment.L(1)
cc_unemployment ~ cc_gdp + cc_unemployment.L(1)
cc_wages ~ cc_unemployment + cc_prices + cc_wages.L(1)
cc_nonenergy_prices ~ cc_ulc + cc_import_prices + cc_unemployment + cc_nonenergy_prices.L(1)
cc_energy_prices ~ oil_price + eur_usd + cc_energy_prices.L(1)
cc_import_prices ~ eur_usd + oil_price + cc_foreign_prices + cc_import_prices.L(1)
cc_export_prices ~ cc_ulc + cc_foreign_prices + cc_export_prices.L(1)
cc_current_account ~ cc_exports + cc_imports + cc_terms_of_trade + cc_current_account.L(1)
cc_government ~ cc_government.L(1) + cc_gdp.L(1)
cc_netborrowing ~ cc_gdp + cc_long_rate + cc_netborrowing.L(1)
cc_credit ~ cc_long_rate + cc_gdp + cc_credit.L(1)
cc_house_prices ~ cc_credit + cc_long_rate + cc_real_income + cc_house_prices.L(1)
cc_spread ~ cc_govdebt + cc_gdp + cc_spread.L(1)

Identities:

cc_gdp == 0.937*cc_domestic_demand + 0.382*cc_exports - 0.33*cc_imports
cc_domestic_demand == 0.579*cc_consumption + 0.211*cc_investment + 0.21*cc_government
cc_foreign_demand == 0.041*at_gdp + 0.04*be_gdp + 0.033*es_gdp + 0.065*fr_gdp + 0.025*ie_gdp + 0.052*it_gdp + 0.074*nl_gdp + 0.098*us_gdp + 0.572*row_gdp
cc_productivity == 1*cc_gdp - 1*cc_employment
cc_ulc == 1*cc_wages - 1*cc_productivity
cc_prices == 0.891298*cc_nonenergy_prices + 0.108702*cc_energy_prices
cc_real_income == 1*cc_wages + 1*cc_employment - 1*cc_prices
cc_competitiveness == 1*cc_export_prices - 1*cc_foreign_prices
cc_terms_of_trade == 1*cc_export_prices - 1*cc_import_prices
cc_govdebt == 1*cc_govdebt.L(1) + 1*cc_netborrowing
cc_long_rate == 1*cc_spread + 1*ea_policy_rate

Where the weights come from:

  • cc_gdp and cc_domestic_demand — average expenditure shares, each one the mean of the period-by-period level ratio (mean(cc_exports / cc_gdp), not the ratio of the means) over this stage’s own estimation window, rounded to 3dp. Computed on levels and used in growth space deliberately: log-linearising an accounting identity turns it into a share-weighted sum of the components’ growth rates, so the level shares are the growth-rate coefficients. The GDP identity holds only up to the national-accounts statistical discrepancy (2–6%, wider for Ireland), and is reported but never flagged for that reason; the consumption/investment/government split sums to exactly 1, because domestic demand is their sum. expenditure_shares().
  • cc_foreign_demand — bilateral trade weights from the ECB WTS matrix, restricted to the modelled partners and loaded on partner GDP. Whatever share of trade the partition does not model is folded onto the exogenous row_gdp residual rather than dropped, so the weights still sum to 1 and the index stays a proper weighted average of growth rates — here 0.572, so over half the index is an assumption that the unmodelled world grows like world GDP. stage2_linkage_weights().
  • cc_prices — HICP basket shares fetched from Eurostat prc_hicp_inw and averaged over the estimation years (0.891 non-energy / 0.109 energy for Germany, not the 0.85/0.15 one would guess). Non-energy plus energy partitions the basket exactly — verified to sum to CP00 in every year 1996–2025 — whereas core plus energy leaves ~19% of the basket unaccounted for. This is the one weight that is genuinely an approximation: HICP weights are re-based annually (the German energy weight ranges 8.8–12.6% over the sample) while a koma identity weight is a constant, so hicp_weights() returns max_deviation to make the size of that approximation visible.
  • cc_long_rate — both weights imposed at exactly 1: a sovereign yield is the policy path plus a term premium, so there is nothing to estimate. This is a rate/none identity, a literal linear combination of levels rather than of growth rates, and identity_consistency() checks it in that space. Note it has two sides — the identity string and the cc_spread series the panel builder constructs — and both derive the policy rate from policy_rate_map(), because when they disagreed the US identity was silently violated by the whole EA–US policy-rate gap (up to 3.25pp).
  • cc_productivity, cc_ulc, cc_real_income — imposed at exactly ±1, because these are definitions rather than estimates: unit labour cost is wages minus productivity, which telescopes through productivity == gdp − employment to nominal wage bill over real output. chain_weighted_index() sums diff(log(x)) * w without renormalising, which is what makes ±1 give exact differences — these reproduce to ~1e-13.
  • cc_govdebt — stock-flow accumulation, both weights exactly 1. The flow is derived so the carry weight can be 1: koma’s injected (w)*x weights are not time-varying, so a debt snowball factor (1+i)/(1+g) cannot be expressed here.

  • new: cc_current_account, cc_government, cc_netborrowing, cc_credit, cc_house_prices, cc_spread, cc_competitiveness, cc_terms_of_trade, cc_govdebt

Stage 3d — Stage 2d + labour block on DE and the REU bloc

k = 60, T = 78, df = 18 · 2005Q1–2024Q4 · 50 stochastic + 33 identities

cc_consumption ~ cc_gdp + cc_long_rate + cc_real_income + cc_consumption.L(1)
cc_investment ~ cc_gdp + cc_long_rate + cc_investment.L(1)
cc_exports ~ cc_foreign_demand + cc_export_prices + cc_foreign_prices + cc_exports.L(1)
cc_imports ~ cc_domestic_demand + cc_imports.L(1)
cc_spread ~ cc_prices + cc_gdp + cc_spread.L(1)
cc_employment ~ cc_gdp + cc_employment.L(1)
cc_unemployment ~ cc_gdp + cc_unemployment.L(1)
cc_wages ~ cc_unemployment + cc_prices + cc_wages.L(1)
cc_nonenergy_prices ~ cc_ulc + cc_import_prices + cc_unemployment + cc_nonenergy_prices.L(1)
cc_energy_prices ~ oil_price + eur_usd + cc_energy_prices.L(1)
cc_import_prices ~ eur_usd + oil_price + cc_foreign_prices + cc_import_prices.L(1)
cc_export_prices ~ cc_ulc + cc_foreign_prices + cc_export_prices.L(1)

Identities:

cc_gdp == 0.932*cc_domestic_demand + 0.406*cc_exports - 0.348*cc_imports
cc_domestic_demand == 0.731*cc_consumption + 0.269*cc_investment
cc_foreign_demand == 0.065*fr_imports + 0.052*it_imports + 0.098*us_imports + 0.104*cn_imports + 0.225*reu_imports + 0.456*row_gdp
cc_long_rate == 1*cc_spread + 1*ea_policy_rate
cc_productivity == 1*cc_gdp - 1*cc_employment
cc_ulc == 1*cc_wages - 1*cc_productivity
cc_prices == 0.8874555*cc_nonenergy_prices + 0.1125445*cc_energy_prices
cc_real_income == 1*cc_wages + 1*cc_employment - 1*cc_prices

Where the weights come from:

  • cc_gdp and cc_domestic_demand — average expenditure shares, each one the mean of the period-by-period level ratio (mean(cc_exports / cc_gdp), not the ratio of the means) over this stage’s own estimation window, rounded to 3dp. Computed on levels and used in growth space deliberately: log-linearising an accounting identity turns it into a share-weighted sum of the components’ growth rates, so the level shares are the growth-rate coefficients. The GDP identity holds only up to the national-accounts statistical discrepancy (2–6%, wider for Ireland), and is reported but never flagged for that reason; without government the domestic-demand split is deliberately inexact — the two shares are renormalised over what is left. expenditure_shares().
  • cc_foreign_demand — bilateral trade weights from the ECB WTS matrix, restricted to the modelled partners and loaded on partner imports. Whatever share of trade the partition does not model is folded onto the exogenous row_gdp residual rather than dropped, so the weights still sum to 1 and the index stays a proper weighted average of growth rates — here 0.456, the smallest residual of any stage, because the US and China are modelled partners here. The reu row is the bloc’s own trade weight, aggregated from its members. stage2_linkage_weights().
  • cc_prices — HICP basket shares fetched from Eurostat prc_hicp_inw and averaged over the estimation years (0.887 non-energy / 0.113 energy for Germany, not the 0.85/0.15 one would guess). Non-energy plus energy partitions the basket exactly — verified to sum to CP00 in every year 1996–2025 — whereas core plus energy leaves ~19% of the basket unaccounted for. This is the one weight that is genuinely an approximation: HICP weights are re-based annually (the German energy weight ranges 8.8–12.6% over the sample) while a koma identity weight is a constant, so hicp_weights() returns max_deviation to make the size of that approximation visible.
  • cc_long_rate — both weights imposed at exactly 1: a sovereign yield is the policy path plus a term premium, so there is nothing to estimate. This is a rate/none identity, a literal linear combination of levels rather than of growth rates, and identity_consistency() checks it in that space. Note it has two sides — the identity string and the cc_spread series the panel builder constructs — and both derive the policy rate from policy_rate_map(), because when they disagreed the US identity was silently violated by the whole EA–US policy-rate gap (up to 3.25pp).
  • cc_productivity, cc_ulc, cc_real_income — imposed at exactly ±1, because these are definitions rather than estimates: unit labour cost is wages minus productivity, which telescopes through productivity == gdp − employment to nominal wage bill over real output. chain_weighted_index() sums diff(log(x)) * w without renormalising, which is what makes ±1 give exact differences — these reproduce to ~1e-13.
  • The reu bloc’s own weights are member-weighted averages, not the bloc series’ own ratios. bloc_expenditure_shares() averages the seven members’ shares; taking mean(reu_exports / reu_gdp) directly would give 1.337 against a true 0.598, because every bloc series is a base-100 chain index and that ratio is just their relative growth since the base period. stage2_shares() aborts rather than falling back, so a bloc without bloc_weights fails loudly. Same rule for its HICP split — bloc_hicp_weights(), since there is no published reu basket to fetch.

Changed from Stage 2d:

  • new: cc_employment, cc_unemployment, cc_wages, cc_nonenergy_prices, cc_energy_prices, cc_import_prices, cc_export_prices, cc_productivity, cc_ulc, cc_real_income
  • cc_consumption: +cc_real_income
  • cc_exports: +cc_export_prices, +cc_foreign_prices
  • cc_prices — now an identity: +cc_nonenergy_prices, +cc_energy_prices, −eur_usd, −oil_price, −cc_gdp, −cc_prices.L(1)

Two things are visible in that sequence and in no single block. The first is that the behavioural forms barely move after stage 2c — 2d changes the partition and not the specification, and 3d adds 3a’s block unchanged — so the differences between those systems are differences of sample and capacity, not of theory. The second is that every step that adds detail spends df, and the df column above falls monotonically until stage 2d re-partitions and buys it back.

The country template — behavioural equations

The model is written once, for a generic country cc, and applied to every economy. That is what makes the equation count manageable: stage 2c has 68 stochastic equations but only eight distinct forms, six of which are these, applied identically eleven times. The forms below are stage 2c’s and stage 2d’s, which are the same; earlier stages differ in the ways set out later.

Six equations per country, identical in form for every economy:

cc_consumption ~ cc_gdp + cc_long_rate + cc_consumption.L(1)
cc_investment ~ cc_gdp + cc_long_rate + cc_investment.L(1)
cc_exports ~ cc_foreign_demand + cc_exports.L(1)
cc_imports ~ cc_domestic_demand + cc_imports.L(1)
cc_prices ~ eur_usd + oil_price + cc_gdp + cc_prices.L(1)
cc_spread ~ cc_prices + cc_gdp + cc_spread.L(1)
  • Estimated in growth-rate space — coefficients on volumes are elasticities
  • long_rate, spread and the policy rates are rates: koma leaves them untransformed, so their coefficients are pp per pp
  • Four COVID impulse dummies (2020Q1–Q3, 2021Q2) enter the five real-side equations; suppressed above for readability

The country template — identities

Enforced during estimation, not fitted. Weights are fixed shares:

cc_gdp == 0.932*cc_domestic_demand + 0.406*cc_exports - 0.348*cc_imports
cc_domestic_demand == 0.731*cc_consumption + 0.269*cc_investment
cc_foreign_demand == 0.065*fr_imports + 0.052*it_imports + 0.098*us_imports + 0.104*cn_imports + 0.225*reu_imports + 0.456*row_gdp
cc_long_rate == 1*cc_spread + 1*ea_policy_rate
  • GDP — expenditure decomposition, exact only up to the statistical discrepancy
  • Domestic demand — absorption; government is out of the system entirely
  • Foreign demand — the trade-weighted external demand index exports load on. This is what links the countries. The weights shown are Germany’s; the partner set and shares are country-specific by construction
  • Long rate — a sovereign yield is the policy path plus a premium; both weights imposed at exactly 1

Plus, once per system

ea_policy_rate ~ ea_prices + ea_gdp + ea_policy_rate.L(1)
us_policy_rate ~ us_prices + us_gdp + us_policy_rate.L(1)   (stage 2b onward)
cn_policy_rate ~ cn_prices + cn_gdp + cn_policy_rate.L(1)   (stage 2d only)

ea_gdp    == sum_i g_i * <member i>_gdp
ea_prices == sum_i g_i * <member i>_prices

There is exactly one ea_policy_rate equation however many euro-area countries the system contains — that is what makes it a genuinely common instrument rather than ten separate ones.

The stages at a glance

Each stage is a deliberate step rather than an iteration on the last. Stages 2a through 2d change the specification or the country partition — never both at once, which is what keeps any pair of them comparable. Stages 3a and 3b add blocks to one country, Germany, and are where the degrees-of-freedom budget finally binds.

Stage Scope Eqs k T df Window
Stage 1 11 countries, estimated separately (k, T, df are per country) 6 + 2 12 78 66 2000Q1–2019Q4
Stage 2a DE + FR, one joint system 13 + 8 19 78 59 2000Q1–2019Q4
Stage 2b 11 countries, one joint system 68 + 35 76 98 22 2000Q1–2024Q4
Stage 2c 11 countries, four refinements 68 + 46 76 98 22 2000Q1–2024Q4
Stage 2d 6 entities: DE FR IT US CN + REU bloc 38 + 25 46 78 32 2005Q1–2024Q4
Stage 3a Stage 2b + German labour/price block 74 + 39 83 98 15 2000Q1–2024Q4
Stage 3b Stage 3a + external/fiscal/financial 79 + 43 90 98 8 2000Q1–2024Q4
Stage 3d Stage 2d + labour block on DE and the REU bloc 50 + 33 60 78 18 2005Q1–2024Q4

Stage 1’s k/T/df are per country — its eleven satellites never share a design matrix. Everything from 2a on is one joint system.

Stages 1 and 2a — the mechanism

Stage 1 — each country its own small system, world variables exogenous.

Stage 2a — DE + FR in one system. Three things change, and they are the whole point:

  • exports driven by partner GDP, not an exogenous world aggregate
  • ea_policy_rate becomes endogenous
  • long_rate enters investment

The finding that set the agenda:

Making the policy rate endogenous did not give it a route to output. Without long_rate in investment it reached only the two long-rate equations — which are terminal.

“A rate rise cannot move GDP.”

Structure has to be traced, not assumed.

Stage 2b — all eleven, and an open loop

68 stochastic equations, 35 identities, k = 76, df = 22.

Tracing what ea_policy_rate can reach within a quarter:

91 of 103 endogenous variables — including every country’s GDP, and itself.

0 of 11 price variables.

The Taylor rule responds to an inflation rate that nothing it does can influence. The monetary block was an open loop, and no amount of estimation would have revealed it — only a structural trace did.

Stage 2c — closing the loop, for free

Four refinements, applied to every country. All four cost zero k — same k = 76, same df = 22 as stage 2b, so the two are directly comparable.

# Refinement Why
1 prices gains gdp the Phillips curve — closes the monetary loop
2 foreign_demand over partner imports partner GDP nets imports out, so it had the wrong sign
3 model the spread, long_rate becomes an identity policy-rate loading straddled zero in all 11
4 consumption gains long_rate a second monetary channel

Result: the policy rate now reaches all 114 endogenous variables, including every price. A fifth refinement was estimated and rejected — it halved in-sample RMSE while gutting the demand elasticity in 9 of 11 countries. Improved fit was the symptom, not the reassurance.

Stage 2c — and what closing the loop cost

In stage 2b prices had no contemporaneous endogenous regressor — it was effectively a univariate AR, and therefore structurally immune to explosive draws. Coupling it to GDP makes it reachable from the policy rate and from everything else that reaches GDP.

Use stage 2c for mechanism, stage 2b for a price fan chart.

Stage 2d — the first stage that buys degrees of freedom

Stage 2c’s equations, a re-partitioned world: DE, FR, IT, US separate, the other seven euro-area economies collapsed into a REU bloc, and China added.

Stage Change k df
Stage 2c 11 countries, refined 76 22
Stage 3a + German labour block 83 15
Stage 3b + external/fiscal/financial 90 8
Stage 2d re-partition to 6 entities 46 32

Every earlier structural change traded df for detail: 22 → 15 → 8. Collapsing seven countries removes enough equations that k falls 76 → 46 — so df rises to 32 even after giving up eighteen quarters of sample.

Stage 2d — China, and what the data does not have

What exists (free, keyless sources):

  • real GDP, SA — World Bank GEM
  • CPI — World Bank GEM
  • merchandise trade volumes — GEM value ÷ price
  • policy rate — OECD IRSTCI
  • trade weights — observed IMF DOTS

What does not exist, anywhere:

Quarterly consumption and investment.

Verified absent from OECD QNA, OECD Economic Outlook, IMF IFS, World Bank GEM, FRED and the NBS itself.

→ the two equations merge into one estimated cn_domestic_demand, rather than being invented from indicator proxies.

Two things stated rather than buried: cn_long_rate is spliced over 45% of the window, and reu_investment is not identified — Ireland’s investment sd is 43.0 and it carries 10.9% of the bloc, so the seven-country average is more volatile than any single member.

Stage 3a / 3b — the wall

Germany gets a labour/wage–price block, then external, fiscal and financial blocks on top.

Stage Adds k df
Stage 2b — 76 22
Stage 3a labour + disaggregated prices (DE only) 83 15
Stage 3b + external, fiscal, financial (DE only) 90 8
  • It cannot be rolled out — on eleven countries. The full block for all of them needs k = 142 against T = 98.
  • At df = 8, de_long_rate’s own lag crossed to 1.004 — explosive — the moment debt became its fifth regressor.
  • A quiet loop is not a stable one: the fiscal–financial cycle showed no explosive draws because one of its links was ~0.

Stage 3c set out to roll these blocks across the euro area and concluded the degrees-of-freedom budget forbade it. That conclusion held for the eleven-country partition; the next slide is what happened when the partition changed.

Stage 3d — the rollout, on the regional core

Stage 3c’s verdict was that further structure needed a longer sample or a smaller system. Stage 2d built the smaller system; stage 3d puts the labour block on it.

Configuration Partition k df Economies covered
DE labour only 11 countries 83 15 1
DE + FR labour 11 countries 90 8 2
DE + REU labour 6 entities 60 18 8
DE + REU + FR + IT 6 entities 74 4 10

The block still costs seven columns per entity. What changed is what a column buys: a bloc covers seven economies for one entity’s worth of k.

And the aggregation is not only a cost. The wage Phillips curve is identified on the bloc (−0.176, interval excluding zero) and not on Germany (−0.105, straddling zero) — the bloc’s unemployment rate carries the crisis-era variation Germany’s does not. What is lost is the institutional coefficients: wage indexation and ULC pass-through both go wrong-signed on the bloc. The bloc has the variation but not the institutions; Germany the reverse.

Forecasts — how they are produced

Adding forecasts was not just a reporting exercise: running every system forward is what turned the degrees-of-freedom argument from a claim about estimation into a measurable property of the output. The caveats below are not boilerplate — each one is a trap that produced a wrong answer before it was handled.

Every system is run 8 quarters forward, 1000 posterior draws.

  • koma silently shortens a horizon whose exogenous series run out — they are extended first, and the delivered horizon is checked
  • koma constrains no draw to be stationary, so explosive draws are filtered and the discarded share is reported
  • Charts show an inner 25–75% band solid and an outer 10–90% band clipped to the panel edge; the untruncated bounds are tabulated
  • Stages 1 and 2a forecast from 2023Q1 (window already observed — a genuine out-of-sample check); stages 2b onward from 2025Q1

Forecast — stage 2d GDP

Forecast — stage 1, against the outturn

The realised path sits inside the band for every country, and the fan widens in exactly the countries you would expect.

Forecast — German GDP, every stage side by side

The charts above show one stage each. This one holds the variable fixed and varies the system, which is the comparison that actually separates the stages: same country, same origin, same eight quarters, same 1000 draws — only the model changes. Stages 1 and 2a are absent because they forecast from 2023Q1, a different origin, and putting them on this axis would compare two different questions.

The medians barely differ – -0.63 to 0.67pp at horizon 8, a spread of 1.3pp. What differs is the width of the band: 51 to 103pp across the same six systems, and it tracks df at a rank correlation of -0.90. The systems disagree far less about where growth is going than about how much they know.

Forecast — German prices, every stage side by side

ImportantThe realised line is not the same in all six panels, and that is not a plotting error

de_prices is two different series across these systems. In stages 2b, 2c and 2d it is observed headline HICP. Under the labour block — stages 3a, 3b and 3d — it becomes an identity over the energy and non-energy sub-indices, built with chain_weighted_index() rather than taken from observed HICP, because observed HICP satisfies a fixed-weight identity only approximately and koma has no identity-consistency check that would catch the difference. The two disagree by up to 0.65pp of quarterly growth, and stage 3d differs again slightly from 3a/3b because its HICP weights are averaged over a different window (0.887/0.113 against 0.891/0.109).

So the top row and the bottom row are forecasting different definitions of German inflation, and only the fans within a row are strictly comparable. common_forecast_variables() detects exactly this and is why de_prices is excluded from the forecast-error scoreboard below.

With that said, the comparison across the first three panels is the stage-2c price finding as a picture. Stage 2b’s cc_prices has no contemporaneous endogenous regressor, so it is effectively a univariate AR with exogenous cost-push terms and is structurally immune to the explosive-draw population. Stage 2c’s Phillips curve couples it to cc_gdp, and prices inherit GDP’s explosive share — which is the price of making prices reachable from the policy rate at all.

Stage 2d 0.004 0.292
Stage 3a 0.009 0.524
Stage 3b 0.020 0.666

Forecast errors — the stages against the outturn

Everything above is about the shape of the predictive distribution. This is about where its centre actually landed. Five quarters of 2025 and 2026 have now been published, so the six systems that forecast from 2025Q1 can be scored on horizons 1 to 5 against realised data none of them saw.

The comparison is only meaningful on a shared variable set, and carrying the same variable name is not enough — the stages have to mean the same thing by it. common_forecast_variables() enforces both halves: it intersects the variable sets, then compares the realised path across stages and drops anything they disagree on. Here that removes three variables:

Variable Largest disagreement in the outturn Why
de_prices 0.6547 pp an identity over the sub-indices under the labour block, observed HICP elsewhere
ea_prices 0.5863 pp inherits de_prices through the euro-area aggregation identity
ea_gdp 0.0024 pp aggregates eleven countries in stage 2b and four in stage 2d

That leaves 23 series — Germany, France, Italy and the US on GDP, consumption, investment, exports and imports, plus French, Italian and US prices. Errors are in rate space, quarterly growth in percentage points; a level error would compound horizon 1’s mistake into every later horizon and would additionally be incomparable for stages 1 and 2a, whose level paths are anchored on filled rather than observed values.

Same 23 series, same origin, and — now checked rather than assumed — the same outturn:

Forecast errors — the numbers

Stage h1 h2 h3 h4 h5 Mean
Stage 2b 1.35 1.26 0.92 0.84 0.95 1.06
Stage 2c 1.41 1.05 1.06 0.77 1.17 1.09
Stage 2d 1.69 0.97 1.00 0.72 1.12 1.10
Stage 3a 1.45 1.05 1.17 0.81 1.25 1.14
Stage 3b 1.46 1.29 1.19 0.76 0.88 1.12
Stage 3d 1.42 0.82 0.96 0.69 0.97 0.97

The spread across stages is small relative to the level of the error – every system is between 0.69 and 1.69pp at every horizon, and the ordering changes from one horizon to the next. Averaged over the five horizons Stage 3d is lowest at 0.97 and Stage 3a highest at 1.14, a gap of 18%. On five quarters and a single origin that ordering is a sanity check, not a ranking.

Forecast errors — what one origin cannot settle

The previous two slides are one draw of the world. This project has already been burned by exactly that: on a five-origin annual sample stage 2c looked better than stage 2b at long horizons, and on a twenty-origin quarterly sample it is clearly worse. A single origin cannot sign a comparison between systems this close together, and the table above should be read as a sanity check that none of them is broken — not as a ranking.

The honest version is an expanding-window backtest that re-estimates every system at every origin. reports/evaluation.qmd runs it: 92 joint-system estimations, twenty usable quarterly origins, four specifications. It predates stages 2d and 3d, so those are absent here.

Twenty origins, re-estimated at each one — the comparison that can carry weight:

The naive AR(1) benchmark explodes past horizon 6 — deliberately unclamped, which is the honest textbook comparison, but it is why RMSE is not readable here and MAE is. Stage 1 beats the joint systems on MAE at every horizon; the joint systems buy cross-country structure, not point accuracy.

Forecast errors — stages 1 and 2a, on their own origin

Stages 1 and 2a forecast from 2023Q1 into a window that is now entirely observed, so they get all eight horizons scored — but against different quarters of history than the six systems above, which is why they are not on the same chart. Their common set is Germany and France only, 12 series.

Stage h1 h2 h3 h4 h5 h6 h7 h8
Stage 1 1.11 1.18 0.46 0.67 0.60 0.62 0.50 0.61
Stage 2a 1.15 1.12 0.51 0.79 0.59 0.57 0.57 0.62

Adding the linkage mechanism (2a) neither helped nor hurt the point forecast at this origin — which is what stage 2a was for. It was a test that the mechanism worked, not a bid for accuracy.

The finding the forecasts made visible

Degrees of freedom are not an abstraction. They are exactly how much of the predictive distribution survives to horizon 8.

Spillovers — stage 2d

Cumulative 8-quarter GDP effect of a +1pp demand shock; rows shocked, columns responding.

de fr it us cn reu
de 1.373 0.385 0.696 0.265 0.274 0.376
fr 1.123 1.387 1.162 0.443 0.442 0.837
it 0.664 0.400 1.208 0.265 0.332 0.486
us 0.834 0.454 0.605 1.155 0.220 0.703

Own effect dominates 6 of 6. China’s row is an order of magnitude smaller than Europe’s — as its trade weights say it should be, now that they come from observed DOTS rather than the reciprocal approximation that would have put 56% of Chinese trade inside the euro area.

Spillovers — is any of it real?

koma has no impulse-response function, so a spillover is the difference between two forecasts — one unconditional, one restricted — paired by common random numbers so the difference isolates the shock rather than koma’s own call-to-call noise. That pairing is exact. What it does not remove is sampling error in the level of the estimand itself, and the only way to find out how large that is, is to re-run the identical battery at a different seed.

Same fit, same battery, only the seed changed:

System Mean |A − B| Max Sign flips
Stage 2b (df 22) 0.350 1.850 7–10 of 30
Stage 2c (df 22) 0.119 0.356 1 of 44
Stage 2d (df 32) 0.108 0.273 0 of 20

For stage 2b, most of what anyone wanted to conclude was smaller than the matrix’s own noise.

Stage 2d is the first system where no off-diagonal cell changes sign when only the seed changes — the concrete payoff of those ten extra degrees of freedom.

What does not work

Check Result
Monetary → GDP (euro area) correctly signed, 6/6 peak negative
Monetary → prices wrong sign — only 1/6 peak negative
Monetary shock on China’s own rule does not work — a horizon-1 adjustment in the rule, not transmission
Oil → prices correctly signed 6/6
Spillover ~ bilateral trade weight fails — Spearman 0.138 against a 0.3 bar

The oil shock is the control: the price block responds sensibly to a cost shock and perversely to a policy rate. That localises the fault to the policy rate’s route in — not to the price equations.

Which system for which question

No single system dominates. The table below is the practical summary; the reason each row is what it is has been given above.

If you want to… Use
understand a mechanism / trace transmission Stage 2c
produce a price fan chart Stage 2b
study EA–US–China spillovers Stage 2d
say anything about Austria, Spain, Ireland… Stage 2b / 2c
model German wages, debt or credit Stage 3a / 3b — Germany only
run a monetary experiment on China nothing here yet

The through-line: every result in this deck that survived did so because it was checked against its own noise floor — a seed placebo, a sign rule, a structural trace, a second specification. The ones that did not survive are in the deck too.
